title: Callbacks to Promises
summary: Why callbacks nest badly, and how a Promise represents a future value.

steps.title: Callbacks
body: The original async style passes a function to call when the work finishes. Node's convention is error first:
Every step nests deeper, and every step must remember to handle errors. Promises fix both problems.

steps.prompt: What are the two main problems with deeply nested callbacks?
options: Code drifts right as steps nest, and error handling must be repeated at each step
They are slower than promises and use more memory
They cannot be used with setTimeout
They run on a separate thread

steps.title: A Promise is a future value
body: A `Promise<T>` is JavaScript's `Task<T>`: an object for a value that will exist later. It is **pending**, then either **fulfilled** with a value or **rejected** with an error, once, forever.
const delay = (ms: number) => new Promise<void>(resolve => setTimeout(resolve, ms));
function getUser(id: number): Promise<{ id: number; name: string }> {
.then(user => user.name.toUpperCase())     // return a value: next .then gets it
.catch(err => console.log(err.message))    // any rejection above lands here
Returning a promise from `.then` chains it, so the steps stay **flat** and one `.catch` covers them all.

steps.explain: A throw rejects the chain, which skips every `.then` until a `.catch`. The catch's return value fulfils the chain again.
